passage:
Before dawn, Irfan unrolled his prayer mat in the corner of the room, careful not to wake his brothers. In the city hostel last year, someone had asked how he could believe anything, and he'd had no good answer. He still didn't. Some mornings he wasn't sure anyone was listening.

But standing there, hands folded, the noise in his head slowed down. The cool floor, the words he'd known since childhood, the first rooster outside. His breathing evened out.

At the well, his neighbour Pooja asked, "Aren't you doubtful these days?"

"Yes," he said. "It still steadies me. I don't need every answer to do it."

Then he added, "But I'll ask the teacher my questions. I don't want to hide behind this."

qa.q: What did Irfan unroll before dawn?
qa.a: Irfan unrolled his prayer mat before dawn.

qa.q: Why does Irfan keep praying even though he is unsure?
qa.a: It steadies him: the noise in his head slows down and his breathing evens out, even on mornings when he isn't sure anyone is listening.

qa.q: Why is asking the teacher a sensible addition to Irfan's prayer?
qa.a: It keeps the practice from becoming a way to avoid his real questions, so he can pray and still ask honestly.

qa.q: What might Pooja be thinking when asking about the doubts?
qa.a: Pooja may be curious or concerned and has noticed something different in Irfan, asking plainly at the well rather than judging.

grounding: Irfan keeps praying despite doubt because it steadies him, and he also plans to ask his questions instead of hiding behind ritual.

passage: Javier hadn't been sure about God since his father's long illness, but every Sunday evening in his tiny Madrid flat he still lit the candle his grandmother had given him and sat in silence for ten minutes. His flatmate Tariq noticed one night. 'I thought you said you don't believe anymore.' Javier shrugged. 'I don't know what I believe. But when I light it, my hands stop shaking. It's like a door into a quiet room.' Tariq sat down on the floor beside him. 'I still pray fajr most mornings, even on days I'm not sure anyone's listening. My uncle says showing up is what matters.' They sat together while the candle burned. After a while Javier added, 'I don't want to use it to hide, though. Last week I lit it just so I wouldn't have to think about Papá.' Tariq nodded. 'Then maybe next Sunday, light it and think about him.'

qa.a: His grandmother gave Javier the candle.

qa.q: How does lighting the candle make Javier feel?
qa.a: It steadies him; his hands stop shaking and he feels calm, even without certainty.
Keeping the practice but using it to face his feelings about his father, not to hide from them.

qa.q: How does Tariq relate to Javier's practice?
qa.a: Tariq understands it, since he still prays fajr on days he isn't sure anyone is listening.

grounding: Shows a young man who still lights a candle despite doubts because it steadies him, while not letting the ritual stand in for facing real questions.

passage: The staff prayer room at the district hospital in Thrissur was barely bigger than a cupboard, with a small brass lamp, a cross on one wall and a framed verse from the Quran on another. Seema, a second-year nursing student, stopped there before every night shift to light the lamp. She wasn't sure anymore what she believed; the ward had shown her too many things she couldn't explain. Joseph, from her batch, found her there at 9:55 one night. 'I didn't know you were religious.' 'I'm not sure I am,' she said. 'But lighting it steadies my hands before the ward. It's the one quiet minute I get.' Joseph nodded. 'I used to say the rosary without believing any of it. Now I just say it.' Seema laughed softly. Then she said, 'But I don't want this to replace asking questions. On my off day I'm going to talk to the chaplain and the old imam who visits. Both.' She went to the ward.

qa.q: At what time did Joseph find Seema in the prayer room?
qa.a: Joseph found her there at 9:55 one night.

qa.q: How does lighting the lamp make Seema feel?
qa.a: It steadies Seema's hands and gives her one calm, quiet minute before the ward.

qa.q: How does Seema keep the ritual from becoming a way to avoid questions?
qa.a: She plans to talk to the chaplain and the visiting imam on her off day.

qa.q: How does Joseph relate to Seema's practice?
qa.a: Joseph understands it, having said the rosary without believing, and now simply saying it.

grounding: Shows a nursing student who keeps lighting a lamp despite doubts because it steadies her, while still making room for real questions.
